sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About When Patients Should Do NGS
sectionToMerge.intro: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) can guide precision cancer treatment, but timing matters. These answers explain when patients may consider NGS testing, which situations benefit most, and what samples and support are involved.

items.q: What is NGS testing in cancer?
items.a: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a laboratory test that analyzes many cancer-related genes at once to detect mutations, fusions, or other alterations that may guide treatment. It is a core tool in precision oncology, helping identify targeted therapy or immunotherapy options and possible eligibility for clinical trials. Whether NGS is appropriate depends on cancer type, stage, and specialist review, and results should always be interpreted by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: When should cancer patients get NGS testing?
items.a: NGS is often considered at the diagnosis of advanced or metastatic cancer, when identifying targetable mutations can shape first-line treatment. It may also be suitable for selected patients with rare cancers, cancers of unknown primary, or disease that has progressed on standard therapy. The right timing depends on cancer type, stage, biomarker profile, and previous treatment. Whether and when to test should be discussed with your treating oncology team.

items.q: Should NGS be done at diagnosis or after treatment fails?
items.a: For many advanced cancers, NGS is increasingly done at diagnosis rather than waiting for treatment to fail, because early results can inform first-line targeted or immunotherapy choices. In some situations, testing after progression helps detect new resistance mutations. The best timing depends on cancer type, tumor stage, available tissue, and specialist judgment. Final decisions about when to test should be made by the treating medical team.

items.q: Which cancers benefit most from NGS testing?
items.a: NGS is especially useful in cancers where targetable mutations are common, such as lung, colorectal, breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and melanoma, as well as cancers of unknown primary. It may also help in rare or aggressive cancers where standard options are limited. The value of testing depends on cancer type, stage, and the likelihood of finding actionable biomarkers. A qualified oncology team can advise whether NGS is likely to change treatment in a specific case.

items.q: Do patients with early-stage cancer need NGS?
items.a: Early-stage cancers do not always require NGS, since standard surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation may be curative without genomic profiling. However, NGS may be considered for selected early-stage patients when it affects treatment choice, such as certain lung or colorectal cancers, or eligibility for trials. The need depends on cancer type, stage, and current guidelines. Whether early-stage testing adds value should be discussed with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Is repeat NGS testing needed if cancer progresses?
items.a: Repeat NGS may be considered when cancer progresses, because tumors can develop new mutations that drive resistance to current therapy. Testing again, sometimes using a fresh biopsy or a blood-based liquid biopsy, may reveal new targeted options. Whether repeat testing is helpful depends on cancer type, prior results, and specialist review. The decision to retest should be guided by the treating oncology team based on the clinical situation.

items.q: What samples or reports are needed for NGS testing?
items.a: NGS testing usually requires a tumor tissue sample, often from an existing biopsy or surgical block, and sometimes a blood sample for liquid biopsy. Pathology reports, prior test results, and a summary of previous treatment help the laboratory and oncologist interpret findings. Sample adequacy and quality can affect whether testing succeeds. Your oncology team and pathologist decide which sample and reports are needed for reliable results.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with NGS testing?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify laboratories or specialists offering NGS testing, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, sample logistics, and follow-up support. Decisions about whether NGS is appropriate, when to test, and how to act on results are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health.
